Probing sub-GeV Dark Matter with conventional detectors

Chris Kouvaris Thanks: kouvaris@cp3.sdu.dk Affiliation: CP3-Origins, University of Southern Denmark, Campusvej 55, DK-5230 Odense, Denmark    Josef Pradler Thanks: josef.pradler@oeaw.ac.at Affiliation: Institute of High Energy Physics, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Nikolsdorfergasse 18, 1050 Vienna, Austria
Abstract

The direct detection of Dark Matter particles with mass below the GeV-scale is hampered by soft nuclear recoil energies and finite detector thresholds. For a given maximum relative velocity, the kinematics of elastic Dark Matter nucleus scattering sets a principal limit on detectability. Here we propose to bypass the kinematic limitations by considering the inelastic channel of photon emission from Bremsstrahlung in the nuclear recoil. Our proposed method allows to set the first limits on Dark Matter below 500​MeV500\,\mathrm{MeV} in the plane of Dark Matter mass and cross section with nucleons. In situations where a Dark Matter-electron coupling is suppressed, Bremsstrahlung may constitute the only path to probe low-mass Dark Matter awaiting new detector technologies with lowered recoil energy thresholds.

Introduction. Weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) are among the theoretically best motivated and experimentally most sought particle candidates for Dark Matter (DM) [1, 2]. The efforts are driven by a broad expectation that physics beyond the Standard Model (SM) should enter near the electroweak scale, with interactions that are not too different from the weak interactions.

There has been a significant amount of experimental effort to push the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to masses below a few GeV. The efforts are hampered by the fact that light DM induces soft nuclear recoils that are difficult to detect unambiguously. In the non-relativistic scattering of a DM particle χ\chi and target nucleus NN with mass mNm_{N}, the three-momentum transfer 𝐪=𝐩χ′−𝐩χ\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}_{\chi}^{\prime}-\mathbf{p}_{\chi} determines the kinetic recoil energy of the nucleus, ER=|𝐪|2/(2​mN)≤2​μN2​v2/mNE_{R}={|\mathbf{q}|^{2}}/({2m_{N}})\leq{2\mu_{N}^{2}v^{2}}/{m_{N}}, where μN\mu_{N} is the DM-nucleus reduced mass and vv is the relative velocity, bounded by the finite gravitational potential of the galaxy. New avenues have therefore been suggested to probe DM below the GeV-scale, such as looking for DM-electron scattering [3] in existing data [4], employing semiconductor targets [5, 6, 7], using superconductors or superfluids [8, 9, 10, 11], nanotubes [12], 2D graphene-like targets [13] and exploiting a non-virialized velocity-component of DM [14].

In this letter we propose a method of probing sub-GeV DM in direct detection by going to the inelastic channel of photon emission from the nucleus in form of Bremsstrahlung11 1 Photon emission from the excitation of low-lying nuclear levels has been considered in [15, 16, 17, 18]. The process requires considerable momentum transfer and concerns electroweak scale DM masses.—an irreducible contribution that accompanies the elastic reaction,

χ+N\displaystyle\chi+N →χ+N⁡(ER)\displaystyle\to\chi+N(E_{R})\, (elastic),\displaystyle\text{(elastic)}, (1a)
χ+N\displaystyle\chi+N →χ+N⁡(ER′)+γ⁡(ω)\displaystyle\to\chi+N(E_{R}^{\prime})+\gamma(\omega)\, (inelastic).\displaystyle\text{(inelastic)}. (1b)

The virtue of considering (1b) is that the available photon energy is bounded by the energy of the relative motion of DM and the target, ω≤μN​v2/2\omega\leq\mu_{N}v^{2}/2, so that we observe a hierarchy for light dark matter,

ER,max=4​(mχ/mN)​ωmax≪ωmax(mχ≪mN).\displaystyle E_{R,\rm max}=4(m_{\chi}/m_{N})\omega_{\rm max}\ll\omega_{\rm max}\quad(m_{\chi}\ll m_{N}). (2)

As we will see, the larger energy deposition in photon emission allows to lower the sensitivity to nuclear recoils to the sub-GeV DM mass regime in present-day detectors. The signal will be be part of the “electron recoil-band” and subject to backgrounds, yet amply detectable: whereas, say, ER=0.5​keVE_{R}=0.5\,\mathrm{keV}, is experimentally easily missed, a photon of energy ω=0.5​keV\omega=0.5\,\mathrm{keV} is hardly ever missed.

Cross section.

It is well known that in the limit of soft photon emission off an electromagnetically charged particle the matrix element for Bremsstrahlung factorizes into the matrix element of elastic scattering MelM_{\rm el} times a manifestly gauge invariant piece. For this to hold in the non-relativistic limit of the emitting particle, the three momentum transfer 𝐪\mathbf{q} in the elastic scattering must be much larger than the change of it due to the additional emission of the photon with momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k}, δ​𝐪=(𝐩N′−𝐩N−𝐤)−(𝐩N′−𝐩N)ω=0\delta\mathbf{q}=(\mathbf{p}_{N}^{\prime}-\mathbf{p}_{N}-\mathbf{k})-(\mathbf{p}_{N}^{\prime}-\mathbf{p}_{N})_{\omega=0}. Hence, imposing |δ​𝐪|≪|𝐪||\delta\mathbf{q}|\ll|\mathbf{q}| yields the soft-photon limit, ω≪|𝐪|​v=2​mN​ER​v≃O⁡(10​keV)​A130​ER1​keV\omega\ll|\mathbf{q}|v=\sqrt{2m_{N}E_{R}}v\simeq O(10\,\mathrm{keV})\sqrt{\frac{A}{130}}\sqrt{\frac{E_{R}}{1\,\mathrm{keV}}}, where AA is the atomic mass number of NN. The latter condition holds well away from the kinematic endpoint of minimum momentum transfer, |𝐪min|≃ω/v|\mathbf{q}_{\rm min}|\simeq\omega/v, and the soft photon limit will be respected. Since ωmax≃μN​v2/2≲|𝐪max|​v\omega_{\rm max}\simeq\mu_{N}v^{2}/2\lesssim|\mathbf{q}_{\rm max}|v holds parametrically, we can further take the approximation ER′≃ERE_{R}^{\prime}\simeq E_{R} in (1b).

The factorization of the matrix element is universal and does not depend on the spin of the nucleus. Summing over the photon polarization, and assuming no directional sensitivity yields a double differential cross section of,

d2​σd​ER​d​ω|naive\displaystyle\left.\frac{d^{2}\sigma}{dE_{R}d\omega}\right|_{\rm naive} =4​Z2​α3​π​1ω​ERmN×d​σd​ER​Θ​(ωmax−ω).\displaystyle=\frac{4Z^{2}\alpha}{3\pi}\frac{1}{\omega}\frac{E_{R}}{m_{N}}\times\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}}\Theta(\omega_{\rm max}-\omega). (3)

Here, d​σ/d​ERd\sigma/dE_{R} is the WIMP-nucleus elastic scattering cross section for (1a), ZZ is the atomic number.

The cross section for Bremsstrahlung emission off a recoiling nucleus gets modified at low photon energies by the fact that it is in a neutral bound state with electrons. The process of photon emission can be viewed as in Fig. 1 where the double line represents the nucleus in the initial (final) atomic state of electrons ii (ff), with intermediate state nn. The matrix element for the transition can be put into the following form,

|Vf​i|2=2​π​ω​|Mel|2\displaystyle|V_{fi}|^{2}=2\pi\omega|M_{\rm el}|^{2} |∑n≠i,f[(𝐝f​n⋅𝐞^∗)​⟨n|e−imemN𝐪⋅∑α𝐫α|i⟩ωn​i−ω\displaystyle\left|\sum_{n\neq i,f}\left[\frac{(\mathbf{d}_{fn}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{*})\matrixelement{n}{e^{-i \frac{m_e}{m_N} \vec q \cdot\sum_{\alpha} \vec r_{\alpha}}}{i}}{\omega_{ni}-\omega}\right.\right.
+(𝐝n​i⋅𝐞^∗)​⟨f|e−imemN𝐪⋅∑α𝐫α|n⟩ωn​i+ω]|2.\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\left.\left.+\frac{(\mathbf{d}_{ni}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{*})\matrixelement{f}{e^{-i \frac{m_e}{m_N} \vec q \cdot\sum_{\alpha} \vec r_{\alpha}}}{n }}{\omega_{ni}+\omega}\right]\right|^{2}. (4)

Here, MelM_{\rm el} is the matrix element for the elastic DM-nucleus collision, 𝐝k​l=e​∑α𝐫α,k​l\mathbf{d}_{kl}=e\sum_{\alpha}\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,kl} is the atomic dipole moment (with sum over the positions 𝐫α\mathbf{r}_{\alpha} of all electrons with elementary charge ee), 𝐞^∗\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{*} is the polarization vector of the photon in three-dimensional transverse gauge, and ωk​l=ωk−ωl\omega_{kl}=\omega_{k}-\omega_{l} is the atomic transition frequency between states |k⟩\ket{k} and |l⟩\ket{l}. The cross section for photon emission will then be given by

d​σ=|Vf​i|2|Mel|2​ω2​d​ω​d​Ω𝐤(2​π)3×d​σel.\displaystyle d\sigma=\frac{|V_{fi}|^{2}}{|M_{\rm el}|^{2}}\frac{\omega^{2}d\omega d\Omega_{\mathbf{k}}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\times d\sigma_{\rm el}. (5)

A few comments regarding (4) are in order. First, the factors 𝐝k​l⋅𝐞^∗\mathbf{d}_{kl}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{*} are part of the dipole transition element V(γ)k​l=−𝐝k​l⋅∂t𝐀∗𝐞,ωV^{(\gamma)}_{kl}=-\mathbf{d}_{kl}\cdot\partial_{t}\mathbf{A}^{*}_{\mathbf{e},\omega} with 𝐀=(2​π/ω)1/2​e−i​ω​t​𝐞^\mathbf{A}=(2\pi/\omega)^{1/2}e^{-i\omega t}\,\hat{\mathbf{e}} (we work in unrationalized units of e2=αe^{2}=\alpha), responsible for the emission of a photon of energy ω\omega. Second, the matrix elements ⟨k|e−imemN𝐪⋅∑α𝐫α|l⟩\matrixelement{k}{e^{-i \frac{m_e}{m_N} \vec q \cdot\sum_{\alpha} \vec r_{\alpha}}}{l} describe the motion of the electron-cloud relative to the nucleus with velocity |𝐯N|=|𝐪|/mN|\mathbf{v}_{N}|=|\mathbf{q}|/m_{N} after the latter receives an impulse 𝐪\mathbf{q} from DM. It is assumed that the kick is to good approximation instantaneous, i.e., the DM-nucleus interaction time τχ∼RN/vχ\tau_{\chi}\sim R_{N}/v_{\chi} is smaller than the time it takes electrons in orbit to adjust to the perturbation, τα∼|𝐫α|/vα\tau_{\alpha}\sim|\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}|/v_{\alpha}. Taking for the nuclear radius RN=1.3​fm​A1/3R_{N}=1.3\,\mathrm{fm}A^{1/3}, a typical DM velocity vχ=10−3v_{\chi}=10^{-3}, and an inner shell electron with radius |𝐫α|=1/(Z​α​me)|\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}|=1/(Z\alpha m_{e}) and velocity vα∼Z​αv_{\alpha}\sim Z\alpha, we get τχ/τα≃10−4​A1/3​Z2\tau_{\chi}/\tau_{\alpha}\simeq 10^{-4}A^{1/3}Z^{2}. Hence our approximation is well justified for light elements; for heavier targets such as xenon, the ratio can become O⁡(1)O(1), but only for the innermost electrons. Going beyond the mentioned approximations requires a dedicated atomic physics calculation, which is certainly welcome but well beyond the scope of this paper. Finally, in the denominators of (4) we neglect any dependence on ERE_{R} based on the fact that ER≪ωn​iE_{R}\ll\omega_{ni}.

On similar grounds as for the dipole matrix element for photon emission, we can make use of the dipole approximation in the boosted matrix elements,

⟨k|e−imemN𝐪⋅∑α𝐫α|l⟩≃−ie​memN​𝐪⋅𝐝k​l(k≠l).\displaystyle\matrixelement{k}{e^{-i \frac{m_e}{m_N} \vec q \cdot\sum_{\alpha} \vec r_{\alpha}}}{l}\simeq\frac{-i}{e}\frac{m_{e}}{m_{N}}\,\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{d}_{kl}\quad(k\neq l). (6)

Here, αr​s​(ω)\alpha_{rs}(\omega) (r,sr,s are cartesian coordinates) denotes the polarizability of an individual atom. In the limit of spherical symmetry, which we will assume henceforth, αr​s​(ω)=α⁡(ω)​δr​s\alpha_{rs}(\omega)=\alpha(\omega)\delta_{rs}. The latter function α⁡(ω)\alpha(\omega) can be related to the atomic scattering factors f⁡(ω)=f1​(ω)+i​f2​(ω)f(\omega)=f_{1}(\omega)+if_{2}(\omega) which are tabulated, α⁡(ω)=−αme​ω2​f​(ω)\alpha(\omega)=-\frac{\alpha}{m_{e}\omega^{2}}f(\omega). By taking the limit in which the atom stays in the ground state, i=fi=f, we neglect further contributions to the photon yield. =4​α3​π​ω​ERmN​|f⁡(ω)|2×d​σd​ER​Θ​(ωmax−ω).\displaystyle=\frac{4\alpha}{3\pi\omega}\frac{E_{R}}{m_{N}}|f(\omega)|^{2}\times\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}}\Theta(\omega_{\rm max}-\omega). (8)

A comparison with (3) exposes nicely the atomic physics modification to the naïve cross section of unscreened Bremsstrahlung emission from the bare nucleus. At low photon energy, the process weakens as ω3\omega^{3} as is typical for dipole emission (the dipole created between the nucleus and electrons). At large energies, f1→Z≫f2f_{1}\to Z\gg f_{2}, the atomic state becomes irrelevant, and (8) approaches (3).

Event rates.

The main idea is to tap the electron recoil that is induced by Bremsstrahlung, when (reliable) experimental sensitivity to nuclear recoils fails at low recoil energy. To arrive at a convenient expression for the differential event rate we neglect the energy deposition ERE_{R} since the respective maximum energies fulfill ER,max≪ωmaxE_{R,\rm max}\ll\omega_{\rm max}, and take the photon energy ω\omega as the only detectable signal, with rate 𝑑σ/𝑑ω=∫ER,minER,maxd​ER​d​σd​ER​d​ωd\sigma/d\omega=\int_{E_{R,\rm min}}^{E_{R,\rm max}}dE_{R}\frac{d\sigma}{dE_{R}d\omega}. The boundaries of the recoil energy integration are found from 3-body kinematics,

ER,max/min\displaystyle E_{R,\rm max/min} =μN2​v2mN​[(1−ωμN​v2)±1−2​ωμN​v2].\displaystyle=\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}v^{2}}{m_{N}}\left[\left(1-\frac{\omega}{\mu_{N}v^{2}}\right)\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{2\omega}{\mu_{N}v^{2}}}\right].

Consider now a standard DM-nucleus recoil cross section, d​σ/d​ER=σ0S​I​mN/(2​μN2​v2)​F2​(|𝐪|)d\sigma/dE_{R}=\sigma^{SI}_{0}m_{N}/(2\mu_{N}^{2}v^{2})F^{2}(|\mathbf{q}|) with spin-independent DM-nucleus cross section σ0S​I≃A2​σn​(μN/μn)2\sigma_{0}^{SI}\simeq A^{2}\sigma_{n}(\mu_{N}/\mu_{n})^{2} where σn\sigma_{n} is the DM-nucleon elastic cross section and μn\mu_{n} the DM-nucleon reduced mass. Making the excellent approximation that the nuclear form factor at low recoil is unity, F2≃1F^{2}\simeq 1, the differential cross section can be integrated to yield,

d​σd​ω=4​α​|f⁡(ω)|23​π​ω​μN2​v2​σ0S​ImN2​1−2​ωμN​v2​(1−ωμN​v2).\displaystyle\frac{d\sigma}{d\omega}=\frac{4\alpha|f(\omega)|^{2}}{3\pi\omega}\frac{\mu_{N}^{2}v^{2}\sigma_{0}^{SI}}{m_{N}^{2}}\sqrt{1-\frac{2\omega}{\mu_{N}v^{2}}}\left(1-\frac{\omega}{\mu_{N}v^{2}}\right). (9)

In a final step, we take the average of the cross section over the velocity distribution of DM in the frame of the detector and compute the event rate,

d​Rd​ω=NT​ρχmχ​∫|𝐯|≥vmind3​𝐯​v​fv​(𝐯+𝐯e)​d​σd​ω.\displaystyle\frac{dR}{d\omega}=N_{T}\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\int_{|\mathbf{v}|\geq v_{\rm min}}d^{3}\mathbf{v}\,vf_{v}(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}_{e})\frac{d\sigma}{d\omega}. (10)

Here, NTN_{T} is the number of target nuclei per unit detector mass and ρχ=0.3​GeV/cm3\rho_{\chi}=0.3\,\mathrm{GeV}/\mathrm{cm}^{3} is the local DM mass density. For fv​(𝐯)f_{v}(\mathbf{v}) we take a truncated Maxwellian with escape speed vesc=544​km/sv_{\rm esc}=544\,\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{s} [19] and most probable velocity v0=220​km/sv_{0}=220\,\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{s}; 𝐯e\mathbf{v}_{e} is the velocity of the Earth relative to the galactic rest frame and vmin=2​ω/μNv_{\rm min}=\sqrt{2\omega/\mu_{N}}.

The penalty for going to the inelastic channel is of course very large. Whereas a factor of α\alpha is compensated by Z2Z^{2} in  (3) [or by f1,22f_{1,2}^{2} in (9)], the factor ER/mNE_{R}/m_{N} may be overcome by a quasi-exponential rising event rate dRel/dER∼e−ER/E0dR_{\rm el}/dE_{R}\sim e^{-E_{R}/E_{0}} with decreasing ERE_{R} where E0=few×keVE_{0}={\rm few}\times\mathrm{keV} for WIMPs and typical target masses. The spill over from photons into the higher energy region is the key that allows us to exploit the inelastic channel in the electron recoil band experimentally.

The prospective parameter space where the method of Bremsstrahlung emission yields an improvement of sensitivity, is best identified by demanding that no elastic nuclear recoil event (with rate d​R/d​ERdR/dE_{R}) has been induced above the detector-specific nominal threshold recoil energy ER,thE_{R,\rm th}, N⁡(ER>ER,th)=exposure×∫ER,th∞d​ER​d​Rd​ER<1N(E_{R}>E_{R,\rm th})={\rm exposure}\times\int_{E_{R,\rm th}}^{\infty}dE_{R}\frac{dR}{dE_{R}}<1, and by computing from there the number of bremsstrahlung-induced electron recoil events via (10). It is important to note that N⁡(ER>ER,th)<1N(E_{R}>E_{R,\rm th})<1 becomes trivially fulfilled for any value of DM-nucleon cross section once the DM mass falls below the kinematic threshold imposed by the maximum relative velocity between DM and target nucleus, vmax=vesc+ve≃750​km/sv_{\rm max}=v_{\rm esc}+v_{e}\simeq 750\,\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{s}. For example, N⁡(ER>ER,th)<1N(E_{R}>E_{R,\rm th})<1 for any value of σ0S​I\sigma_{0}^{SI} once the DM mass falls below 3.3​GeV3.3\,\mathrm{GeV} in a xenon experiment with nominal threshold of ER,th=1.1​keVE_{R,\rm th}=1.1\,\mathrm{keV} such as in LUX [20, 21] and before accounting for finite detector resolution. Figure 2 shows the theoretical rates for elastic scattering, d​R/d​ERdR/dE_{R}, and the photon emission rate d​R/d​ωdR/d\omega as labeled resultant from nuclear recoils of a DM particle of mass mχ=1​GeVm_{\chi}=1\,\mathrm{GeV} and a DM-nucleon cross section of σn=10−35​cm2\sigma_{n}=10^{-35}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}. The dotted line is the rate according to the naive estimate (3).

Probing low-mass DM.

We now explore the sensitivity to Bremsstrahlung in the usual (mχ,σn)(m_{\chi},\sigma_{n}) plane. Here we focus on the ionization-only signal in liquid scintillator experiments, for which XENON10 [26], and most recently XENON100 [27], have presented results. The ionization threshold of xenon is ∼12​eV\sim 12\,\mathrm{eV}, hence the emission of a 100 eV photon can already produce multiple ionized electrons.

For XENON10 the collaboration has reported the spectrum in number of electrons, and we compute the electron yield upon absorption of the Bremsstrahlung photon following [4, 28] and assuming that it takes on average 13.8 eV to produce an ionized electron [29]; a simliar, albeit simplified program has been carried out in [30, 31]. For XENON100 we convert the expected ionization signal into photoelectrons (PE) using a yield of 19.7​PE/e−19.7~{\rm PE}/e^{-} and a width of 7​PE/e−7~{\rm PE}/e^{-} [27]; the conversion corresponds to 1.43​PE/eV1.43\,~{\rm PE}/\mathrm{eV}. Although signal formation at lowest energies is poorly understood, a recent measurement at 200​eV200\,\mathrm{eV} electron recoil energy supports such naive expectations of charge yield, with recombination of ions and electric field dependence playing little role [32, 33]. We then place a limit using the “pmaxp_{\rm max}” method [34, 26]. The respective sensitivities to σn\sigma_{n} are shown in Fig. 3 by the (blue and orange) shaded region as labeled. A thin orange line in the XENON100 region shows the limit with the (ad-hoc) pessimistic choice of 30 eV/electron and resulting conversion factor 0.6​PE/eV0.6\,~{\rm PE}/\mathrm{eV}. Finally, we note that LUX may soon improve on the XENON100 limit, because of lower electron backgrounds [35]. We estimate (supported by our own Monte Carlo simulation; see also [36, 37, 38, 39]) that for σn≳10−30​cm2\sigma_{n}\gtrsim 10^{-30}\,\mathrm{cm}^{2} the limits become invalidated as elastic scattering of DM inside the Earth slowly degrades energy and flux of the incident particles; the corresponding approximate demarcation line is labeled “m.f.p.”.

Importantly, the next generation of dual-phase liquid scintillator direct detection experiments, such as XENON1T [40] and LZ [41], are coming online or are being planned. Although a much reduced electromagnetic recoil background may be expected, Rb.g.=10−4−10−5/kg/day/keVR_{\rm b.g.}=10^{-4}-10^{-5}\,/\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{day}/\mathrm{keV} [40], such rate requires volume fiducialization. The latter is accomplished through the much weaker scintillation signal S1 with an overall detection efficiency of only ∼10%\sim 10\%. Hence, improvement over current limits is not guaranteed, and instead we advocate a dedicated smaller setup with both, high S1 light collection efficiency and single photon sensitivity [42]; see also recent Ref. [43]. We estimate a principle limit for this technology in Fig. 3, assuming Rb.g.=10−4/kg/day/keVR_{\rm b.g.}=10^{-4}\,/\mathrm{kg}/\mathrm{day}/\mathrm{keV} with an exposure of 600600 kg-yr and requiring two S1 photons produced at 10% with respect to ionized electrons and each of the S1 photons detected with 40%-100% efficiency (varying the efficiency determines the thickness of the red band). Finally, solid state scintillators have reached O⁡(100​eV)O(100\,\mathrm{eV}) thresholds, most notably CRESST-II with the only reported DM-nucleon cross section limit below 1​GeV1~\mathrm{GeV} [22]. We exemplify the near-future reach by following the experiment’s own projections [44] with threshold 100​eV100\,\mathrm{eV}, a factor of 100 reduced backgrounds, and neglecting efficiencies for simplicity.

Comparison to DM-electron scattering.

MeV-mass DM is already constrained through scattering on electrons and the resulting ionization signal [3, 4]. Hence, best progress from our proposals can be expected in “leptophobic” models with suppressed (or absent) DM couplings to electrons. One of the simplest leptophobic models is DM coupled to the SM through a light U​(1)BU(1)_{B} gauge boson VμV_{\mu},

ℒ⟩\⊔\displaystyle{\cal L_{\rm int}} =gB​(Vμ​JμB−χ¯​V̸​χ)−κ2​Vμ​ν​Fμ​ν.\displaystyle=g_{B}(V^{\mu}J^{B}_{\mu}-\bar{\chi}\not{V}\chi)-\frac{\kappa}{2}V^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}. (11)

with gBg_{B} the U​(1)BU(1)_{B} gauge coupling (charge), JBμ≡13​∑iq¯i​γμ​qiJ_{B}^{\mu}\equiv\tfrac{1}{3}\sum_{i}\bar{q}_{i}\gamma^{\mu}q_{i} is the baryon current (with the sum over all quark species). Even if κ=0\kappa=0 at the tree level, DM-electron scattering may be induced radiatively, giving parametrically, if no cancellation occurs, κrad∼e​gB/(16​π2).\kappa_{\rm rad}\sim eg_{B}/(16\pi^{2}). This would lead to a ratio of cross sections of DM-electron over DM-nucleon scattering as σe/σn=α​κrad2/αB∼α2/16​π2∼3×10−7{\sigma_{e}}/{\sigma_{n}}={\alpha\kappa_{\rm rad}^{2}}/{\alpha_{B}}\sim{\alpha^{2}}/{16\pi^{2}}\sim 3\times 10^{-7}, which demonstrates that a large hierarchy can be achieved in this simple model; σn≃16​π​αB2​mχ2​mV−4\sigma_{n}\simeq{16\pi\alpha_{B}^{2}m_{\chi}^{2}}{m_{V}^{-4}} for mV2≫𝐪2m_{V}^{2}\gg\mathbf{q}^{2}. This is exemplified in Fig. 4 where we compare the rate of Bremsstrahlung emission to the rate of DM-electron scattering d​R/d​ER,edR/dE_{R,e} for mχ=400​MeVm_{\chi}=400\,\mathrm{MeV}. Any detailed analysis of electron multiplicity upon either scattering process will likely improve the sensitivity to Bremsstrahlung because of a higher primary energy of the photon.

The model of gauged baryon number is constrained in a number of ways, notably from monojet production at colliders [45], from missing energy contributions to rare meson decays [25], and from cosmology; further, model-dependent constraints arising from the UV-completion of U​(1)BU(1)_{B} are obtained in [46]. For illustration, in Fig. 3 we pick mV=300​MeVm_{V}=300\,\mathrm{MeV}, compatible with flavor constraints, and show the ensuing collider limit which comes in this case from CDF. Finally, MiniBOONE may probe the window on large αB\alpha_{B} and MeV-scale mVm_{V} in the near future [25].

Conclusions.

In this letter we show that the irreducible contribution of photon emission in the ordinary process of elastic DM-nucleus scattering, “Bremsstrahlung,” opens up the possibility to probe sub-GeV DM with present-day technology and conventional detectors. The photon endpoint energy is the kinetic energy of DM, and we derive the first limits on DM-nucleon scattering for mχ<500​MeVm_{\chi}<500\,\mathrm{MeV}.

Further progress along the lines suggested here can be made. First, atomic physics calculations should allow to quantify contributions to photon emission from excited final states of the atom. Second, there is an additional contribution to the electron yield from the “shake-off” of electrons in the elastic scattering [47]. Third, the spin-dependent case should be investigated. Fourth, signal formation in materials with band structure, where single-atom polarizability is inadequate, should be investigated. Fifth, photon emission in coherent neutrino nucleus scattering should be included in direct detection neutrino background estimates. A number of these points will be addressed in an upcoming paper [48].
